questions.q: A team runs a MongoDB app on EC2 and wants a managed AWS database with the fewest code changes. Documents are up to 5 MB and the app runs aggregation pipelines on many fields. Which service fits?

options.t: DynamoDB
options.why: Wrong: items are limited to 400 KB and the data model would need a redesign.

options.t: Amazon DocumentDB
options.why: Right: it speaks the MongoDB API and drivers, allows 16 MiB documents and supports aggregation pipelines.

options.t: Aurora PostgreSQL
options.why: Wrong: a relational model means rewriting the data layer.

options.t: OpenSearch Service
options.why: Wrong: it is a search engine, not the primary store for a MongoDB app.

questions.explain: MongoDB compatibility plus large documents and ad hoc queries points to DocumentDB.
questions.remember: MongoDB drivers and queries with minimal change, or documents over 400 KB with ad hoc queries → DocumentDB. Key-based access at massive serverless scale → DynamoDB.
variants: Known key lookups, spiky traffic, no sizing wanted → DynamoDB on-demand.
Joins and strict relational integrity → Aurora or RDS.
Graph traversal → Neptune.

questions.q: A DocumentDB application sends heavy read traffic and the primary is busy. The team wants reads served by replicas without changing the endpoint on failover. What should they do?

options.t: Connect every client to the cluster endpoint with the default read preference
options.why: Wrong: the cluster endpoint always points to the primary, so reads stay on it.

options.t: Connect to each replica's instance endpoint
options.why: Wrong: instance endpoints break on failover and are not for app use.

options.t: Use the cluster endpoint with replicaSet=rs0 and readPreference=secondaryPreferred
options.why: Right: reads go to replicas and writes to the primary, and failover stays transparent.

options.t: Put an Application Load Balancer in front of the instances
options.why: Wrong: the reader endpoint and replica set mode already handle this, and an ALB does not speak the MongoDB protocol.

questions.explain: Replica set mode with secondaryPreferred offloads reads to replicas.
questions.remember: Reads to replicas: replica set mode with secondaryPreferred, or the reader endpoint. Writes always go through the cluster endpoint to the primary.
variants: Need one specific replica for analytics → its instance endpoint, ideally a dedicated replica.
Engine older than 8.0.2 → also add retryWrites=false.
Reader endpoint balances connections, not queries.

questions.q: A mobile app has spiky, unpredictable traffic. The team wants MongoDB compatibility but does not want to pick instance sizes. Which DocumentDB option fits?

options.t: Elastic cluster
options.why: Wrong: elastic clusters shard for huge write and read scale, they are not the answer to unsized spiky load.

options.t: db.t3.medium burstable instance
options.why: Wrong: it is for dev/test with limited connections and does not scale with load.

options.t: A global cluster
options.why: Wrong: it adds Regions for DR and local reads, not capacity sizing.

options.t: DocumentDB Serverless (db.serverless)
options.why: Right: capacity scales in DCUs and is billed per second, which suits spiky load.

questions.explain: Serverless scales compute with demand without disrupting transactions.
questions.remember: Spiky or unsized MongoDB-style workload → DocumentDB Serverless (DCUs). Write scale beyond the largest primary → elastic cluster.
variants: Writes outgrow the biggest primary → elastic cluster with a shard key.
Steady predictable load → provisioned instances (Reserved Instances).
Dev/test only → single instance or burstable class.

questions.q: A DocumentDB primary is at its largest instance size and write throughput is still too low. Data is expected to reach petabytes. What is the best change?

options.t: Add 15 read replicas
options.why: Wrong: replicas are read-only, so write throughput does not improve.

options.t: Move to an elastic cluster and choose a shard key with many unique values
options.why: Right: elastic clusters shard writes across up to 32 shards, and a high-cardinality key avoids hot shards.

options.t: Switch the storage configuration to I/O-Optimized
options.why: Wrong: it removes per-I/O charges but does not raise write capacity.

options.t: Enable a global cluster
options.why: Wrong: only the primary Region accepts writes, so write capacity stays the same.

questions.explain: Elastic clusters are how DocumentDB scales writes out.
questions.remember: Reads scale with replicas (up to 15); writes scale up the primary, then out with an elastic cluster and a good shard key.
variants: Poor shard key such as low-cardinality values → hot shards.
Migrating a sharded MongoDB cluster → elastic cluster.
Only more read capacity needed → add replicas.

questions.q: A team stores embeddings in DocumentDB for semantic search on 5.0 instance-based clusters. Recall matters most, the collection may be empty at index creation, and no training step is wanted. Which index fits?

options.t: IVFFlat
options.why: Wrong: it clusters existing data into lists, so it should be created after data is loaded.

options.t: A compound index on the embedding and a category field
options.why: Wrong: vector indexes do not support compound options.

options.t: A sparse vector index
options.why: Wrong: sparse options are not supported for vector indexes.

options.t: HNSW
options.why: Right: best recall and query speed, no training step, and it can be built on an empty collection.

questions.explain: HNSW suits an empty collection and high recall.
questions.remember: Best recall, build on an empty collection → HNSW. Cheaper, faster build and data already loaded → IVFFlat. No index → exact (slow) search.
variants: Data already loaded and cheap build wanted → IVFFlat.
No vector index at all → exact nearest-neighbour search.
Aurora PostgreSQL equivalent → pgvector HNSW or IVFFlat.

questions.q: A production DocumentDB cluster must survive an AZ failure with a fast, predictable failover. What is the best design?

options.t: A single instance, since storage is copied 6 ways across 3 AZs
options.why: Wrong: storage is durable but compute is lost, and recreating a primary is slow.

options.t: One primary and replicas of the same class in at least three AZs, with failover priority tiers set
options.why: Right: a replica is promoted quickly and tiers choose which one goes first.

options.t: Two instances in the same AZ
options.why: Wrong: an AZ failure takes both down.

options.t: Frequent manual snapshots
options.why: Wrong: snapshots protect data but do not give failover.

questions.explain: Storage is already multi-AZ; compute availability comes from replicas.
questions.remember: Compute HA = replicas in different AZs (minimum 2 instances in 2 AZs, production 3 in 3). Multi-AZ is not a backup.
variants: Cross-Region DR with RPO in seconds → global cluster.
Only one instance fails → DocumentDB creates a new primary, much slower than promoting a replica.
Replica is smaller than the primary → failover can reduce performance.

questions.q: A developer drops an important collection by mistake at 14:05. Automated backups are enabled with 7-day retention. What is the correct recovery?

options.t: Use Backtrack to rewind the cluster
options.why: Wrong: DocumentDB has no Backtrack-style rewind.

options.t: Fail over to a replica
options.why: Wrong: replicas copy the same mistake.

options.t: Restore the cluster in place to 14:04
options.why: Wrong: restores never overwrite the cluster.

options.t: Point-in-time restore to just before 14:05 into a new cluster, then copy the data back or switch the app
options.why: Right: PITR always creates a new cluster within the retention window.

questions.explain: PITR makes a new cluster; there is no in-place rewind.
questions.remember: Accidental delete → PITR (to about the last 5 minutes, retention 1-35 days) into a new cluster. Older than the window → a manual snapshot.
variants: Need an archive for 1 year → manual snapshots or mongodump to S3; PITR max is 35 days.
Failover or replicas never protect against logical errors.
After restore, re-add instances and update connection strings.

questions.q: Analysts need read-only access to a single DocumentDB database. The security team requires least privilege and no use of the primary user. What should the admin do?

options.t: Create a user in admin with the read role on that database
options.why: Right: built-in RBAC roles scope read access to one database.

options.t: Share the primary user credentials
options.why: Wrong: the primary user should not be used in apps and has broad rights.

options.t: Grant readAnyDatabase
options.why: Wrong: it is cluster-wide, which is more than needed.

options.t: Add an IAM policy allowing read on the cluster
options.why: Wrong: IAM policies do not grant MongoDB data rights, and IAM auth is a login method that maps to DocumentDB users.

questions.explain: The read role on one database is the least-privilege fit.
questions.remember: Per-database access → RBAC: read or readWrite on that database. Custom single-collection actions → user-defined role. Users live in the admin database.
variants: Access to one collection only → user-defined role with specific actions such as find.
Password-less access from Lambda → IAM authentication (5.0 instance-based, MONGODB-AWS).
Cluster-wide read → readAnyDatabase.

questions.q: Auditors want to know who dropped collections in DocumentDB. The team set the cluster parameter audit_logs to ddl, but no events appear in CloudWatch Logs. What is missing?

options.t: Enable CloudWatch Logs export for the audit log type on the cluster
options.why: Right: auditing needs both the parameter and the log export.

options.t: Enable CloudTrail data events
options.why: Wrong: CloudTrail logs management API calls, not MongoDB operations.

options.t: Turn on the profiler
options.why: Wrong: the profiler logs slow operations, not audit events.

options.t: Switch to I/O-Optimized storage
options.why: Wrong: storage configuration has nothing to do with audit logs.

questions.explain: Auditing is a two-step setup: parameter plus log export.
questions.remember: No audit logs → one of two steps was skipped: audit_logs parameter, or CloudWatch Logs export for audit. CloudTrail only sees management API calls.
variants: Too much DML noise → setAuditConfig filters by user, command or namespace.
Who called ModifyDBCluster → CloudTrail.
Audit values: ddl, dml_read, dml_write, all, none (default).

questions.q: A search index in OpenSearch must stay in sync with a DocumentDB collection in near real time. Which approach fits?

options.t: Run mongodump nightly and reload the index
options.why: Wrong: a batch export is far from near real time.

options.t: Enable change streams on the collection and process events with Lambda into OpenSearch
options.why: Right: change streams provide time-ordered change events, which are disabled by default and enabled per collection.

options.t: Enable audit_logs=dml_write and parse the logs
options.why: Wrong: audit logs are for compliance, not change data capture.

options.t: Use the reader endpoint to poll all documents
options.why: Wrong: polling is wasteful and misses deletes.

questions.explain: Change streams are the CDC feature in DocumentDB.
questions.remember: Keep another system in sync with DocumentDB → change streams (enable per collection; default retention 3 hours, up to 7 days) feeding Lambda, then OpenSearch or others.
variants: Online MongoDB migration → DMS full load plus CDC.
Event too large (over 16 MB) → $changeStreamSplitLargeEvent on 8.0.2+.
Engine 3.6/4.0 → read change streams from the primary only.
